Which AI Assistant, Which Seats

The Build OrderPart 6

By lowob · 12 July 2026 · 9-minute read · Strategy

Most firms choose an AI assistant by comparing model benchmarks, then buy seats for everyone. Both choices are usually wrong. The model is the fastest-changing layer of the stack and the least sticky; what lasts is how well the assistant fits your suite, reaches your systems, respects your controls and records what it did. And seats bought ahead of a workflow go unused. Buy for the people in the first commercial workflow, and expand on evidence.

Choosing a business AI assistant has become a ritual of comparison tables and benchmark scores. A team reads which model leads this month's leaderboard, runs a few prompts, and signs for enough seats to cover the company. Three months later, weekly use has settled at a fraction of seats, and the leaderboard has changed.

The problem is not the choice of model. It is treating the model as the decision.

The model is the least sticky layer

Every layer of the brain changes at a different speed. The suite (Google Workspace or Microsoft 365) changes over years. The CRM changes over years. The record of decisions should outlive them both. The model underneath an assistant changes every few months.

The market already reflects this. Microsoft added Anthropic's Claude models to Microsoft 365 Copilot in 2026, and reporting on the paid Copilot tier described model choice as its standout addition. When the largest assistant vendor lets customers pick the model inside its product, the model has become a setting rather than a platform.

Spending data points the same way. Menlo Ventures' December 2025 survey of enterprise decision-makers put Anthropic at about 40% of enterprise large-language-model spend, OpenAI at 27% and Google at 21%; Menlo is an investor in Anthropic, and we note that. Card-spend data from Ramp, reported in mid-2026, showed Anthropic and OpenAI each paid for by roughly two-fifths of US businesses with AI subscriptions. Different methods, similar conclusion: buyers use more than one provider, and leadership shifts.

What to compare instead

CriterionQuestion to askWhy it lasts
Suite fitHow deeply does it read our email, files and meetings?The suite changes slowly; native access beats bolt-ons
ConnectorsDoes it connect to our CRM and documents natively or through MCP servers?Open-standard connectors survive a change of assistant
Admin and data controlsCan we set who sees what, control retention and exclude data from training?Controls are what security review will test
LoggingCan we export what it was asked, what it saw and what it produced?The gate in Part 8 depends on it
Agent supportCan it run multi-step tasks with tools and approval pauses?Determines how far up the autonomy dial it can go
Model choiceCan we change the underlying model without changing the product?Protects against leaderboard churn

Vendor capabilities change quickly, so any comparison table is a snapshot. We would rather give buyers the questions than a ranking that will be wrong next quarter. Our guide The pilot that survives security review covers the controls in more depth.

How the main options line up, in general terms

OptionNatural fitWatch for
Microsoft 365 CopilotFirms running on Microsoft 365, with data in SharePoint, Outlook and TeamsPaid add-on pricing per user; weekly use after rollout
Gemini for Google WorkspaceFirms running on Google WorkspaceCoverage of non-Google systems through connectors
ChatGPT (business tiers)Teams wanting a general assistant across toolsDepth of connection into the suite of record
Claude (business tiers)Teams doing long-form analysis, writing and agentic work with MCP connectorsDepth of connection into the suite of record

None of these is the right answer for every firm, and several firms will reasonably run two: a suite-native assistant for everyday work and a second for heavier analysis or agent building. The test is whether each seat has a job.

Fewer seats, more wiring

The adoption record argues for starting small. Fewer than 4.5% of Microsoft 365's roughly 450 million commercial customers pay for Copilot, and only 20% to 30% of payers use it weekly, according to figures reported by Windows Latest in July 2026. Microsoft separately reported around 30 million paid seats. A large absolute number and a small share of the base: both are true, and both suggest that seats without a workflow drift.

The alternative is to buy for the commercial cohort only: the people in the first workflow chosen at Gateway 0. Wire the assistant into their email, calendar and CRM first (Part 5). Measure weekly active use and the workflow's own measure, such as hours of meeting preparation. Expand seat by seat where both move.

Buy seats for a workflow, not for a headcount.

The cost question

Seat prices are visible; the larger costs are not. Microsoft's pricing page listed Microsoft 365 Copilot Business at $21 per user per month on annual billing in November 2026, on top of an existing Microsoft 365 licence, and the other assistants publish similar business tiers. For a cohort of twenty people that is a modest line. The cost that matters is unused seats across a whole company, and the time spent rolling out an assistant nobody was asked to use for anything in particular. Our analysis Seats, usage or outcomes covers how AI vendors price, and why usage-based billing is spreading.

Illustrative example: right-sizing the seats
Decision
Cut assistant seats from company-wide to the 18 people in the commercial workflow, and wire those seats into email, calendar and CRM first.
Reason and owner
Weekly use across company-wide seats was low and flat; nobody had a defined task. Owned by the head of operations.
What changed
Weekly use in the cohort is tracked alongside meeting preparation time; seats are added team by team where both improve.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size professional services firm, built from patterns across engagements.

lowob takeaways

  • Do not choose by leaderboard. The model is the layer most likely to change next quarter.
  • Choose by fit, connectors, controls and logs. These outlast any single model.
  • Expect to run more than one. Many firms reasonably use a suite-native assistant plus one for heavier work.
  • Buy for a workflow. Seats follow evidence, not headcount.
Gateway card

Before you buy seats

  • The first workflow and its cohort named
  • Suite fit and connectors to CRM and documents confirmed
  • Admin, retention and training-data controls checked
  • Logging of prompts, sources and outputs available
  • Weekly use and the workflow measure set up before rollout

Common questions

Which AI assistant is best for business?

It depends less on the model than on fit: the assistant that reads your suite natively, connects to your CRM and documents, meets your controls and logs its work is usually the right first choice. Many firms reasonably run two.

Should we buy Microsoft 365 Copilot for everyone?

Usually not at first. Buy for the people in the first workflow, wire the assistant into their systems, and expand where weekly use and the workflow measure both improve.

Can Microsoft Copilot use Claude models?

Yes. Microsoft added Anthropic's Claude models to Microsoft 365 Copilot in 2026, making the model a choice within the product.

How should we compare ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot?

Compare suite fit, connector depth and MCP support, administrative and data controls, logging, agent support and model choice. Benchmark rankings change too often to anchor a purchase.

Next move

Count your assistant seats and your weekly active users. If the ratio is poor, the fix is rarely a different model; it is a defined workflow and a smaller cohort.
